_note: Every entry was checked against a publisher, journal, or library record. 'url' points to that record. Fields left out were not confirmed.

general.cite: Plofker, K. (2009). Mathematics in India: 500 BCE–1800 CE. Princeton University Press. ISBN 9780691120676.
general.why: The standard scholarly survey of the field.

general.cite: Joseph, G. G. (2011). The Crest of the Peacock: Non-European Roots of Mathematics (3rd ed.). Princeton University Press. ISBN 9780691135267.
general.why: Widely cited history of non-European mathematics, with chapters on India and the Jaina school.

general.cite: Colebrooke, H. T. (trans.) (1817). Algebra, with Arithmetic and Mensuration, from the Sanscrit of Brahmegupta and Bháscara. London: John Murray.
general.why: The first English translation of Brahmagupta's and Bhāskara II's arithmetic and algebra.

pingala.cite: van Nooten, B. (1993). Binary numbers in Indian antiquity. Journal of Indian Philosophy, 21, 31–50.
pingala.why: The classic study of Pingala's binary enumeration of meters. (Link: Kulkarni's paper, which cites it.)

pingala.cite: Kulkarni, A. (2008). Recursion and Combinatorial Mathematics in Chandashastra. arXiv:math/0703658.
pingala.why: Reads Pingala's sutras 8.20–8.35 (prastara, nashta, uddishta, meru) as recursive algorithms.

pingala.cite: Singh, P. (1985). The so-called Fibonacci numbers in ancient and medieval India. Historia Mathematica, 12, 229–244.
pingala.why: Traces the mātrā-meter counts 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … through Virahāṅka, Gopāla, Hemacandra and Nārāyaṇa.

pingala.cite: Halāyudha (10th c.). Mṛtasañjīvanī, commentary on Pingala's Chandaḥśāstra. Dating per Winternitz, History of Indian Literature, vol. III.
pingala.why: The commentary that makes the meru-prastāra (Pascal's triangle) explicit.

pingala.cite: Gray, F. (1953). Pulse code communication. US Patent 2,632,058 (filed 1947).
pingala.why: The reflected binary code the walk follows.

madhava.cite: Rajagopal, C. T., & Rangachari, M. S. (1978). On an untapped source of medieval Keralese mathematics. Archive for History of Exact Sciences, 18(2), 89–102. doi:10.1007/BF00348142
madhava.why: Landmark paper bringing the Kerala series for π and arctan to modern attention.

madhava.cite: Roy, R. (1990). The discovery of the series formula for π by Leibniz, Gregory and Nilakantha. Mathematics Magazine, 63, 291–306.
madhava.why: Prize-winning comparison of the European and Kerala derivations.

madhava.cite: Sarma, K. V., Ramasubramanian, K., Srinivas, M. D., & Sriram, M. S. (2008). Gaṇita-Yukti-Bhāṣā (Rationales in Mathematical Astronomy) of Jyeṣṭhadeva, Vols. I–II. Springer. ISBN 978-1-84882-072-2.
madhava.why: Critical edition and translation of the Malayalam text that gives the proofs.

madhava.cite: Ramasubramanian, K. (2023). The history and historiography of the discovery of calculus in India. Proceedings of the ICM 2022, EMS Press, 5784–5812. doi:10.4171/ICM2022/77
madhava.why: Invited survey at the International Congress of Mathematicians.

madhava.cite: Ramanujan, S. (1914). Modular equations and approximations to π. Quarterly Journal of Mathematics, 45, 350–372.
madhava.why: The fast series behind modern π records.

madhava.cite: Tom's Hardware (2025). Pi calculating record shattered at 314 trillion digits with a four-month run on a single server.
madhava.why: The current record computation of π.

madhava.cite: Udrescu, S.-M., & Tegmark, M. (2020). AI Feynman: A physics-inspired method for symbolic regression. Science Advances, 6(16), eaay2631.
Raayoni, G., et al. (2021). Generating conjectures on fundamental constants with the Ramanujan Machine. Nature, 590, 67–73.
madhava.why: Computer search for formulas for π and e.

chakravala.cite: Selenius, C.-O. (1975). Rationale of the chakravāla process of Jayadeva and Bhāskara II. Historia Mathematica, 2, 167–184.
chakravala.why: Shows the method is a minimal-length, best-approximation continued-fraction algorithm; for N = 61 it needs a handful of steps where the European route needs about 22 convergents.

chakravala.cite: Lenstra, H. W. (2002). Solving the Pell equation. Notices of the American Mathematical Society, 49(2), 182–192.
chakravala.why: How the equation is solved today.

chakravala.cite: Hallgren, S. (2007). Polynomial-time quantum algorithms for Pell's equation and the principal ideal problem. Journal of the ACM, 54(1), Article 4.

ramanujan.cite: Hardy, G. H., & Ramanujan, S. (1918). Asymptotic formulae in combinatory analysis. Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (2), 17, 75–115.
ramanujan.why: The paper that founded the circle method and gave the asymptotic formula for p(n).

ramanujan.cite: Andrews, G. E., & Berndt, B. C. (2005). Ramanujan's Lost Notebook, Part I. Springer.
ramanujan.why: The definitive edition of the lost notebook, with proofs.

ramanujan.cite: Ono, K. (2000). Distribution of the partition function modulo m. Annals of Mathematics, 151(1), 293–307.
ramanujan.why: Congruences for every prime from 5 upward.

ramanujan.cite: Bruinier, J. H., & Ono, K. (2013). Algebraic formulas for the coefficients of half-integral weight harmonic weak Maass forms. Advances in Mathematics, 246, 198–219.
ramanujan.why: A finite algebraic formula for p(n).

sriyantra.cite: Kulaichev, A. P. (1984). Sriyantra and its mathematical properties. Indian Journal of History of Science, 19(3).
sriyantra.why: Treats the construction as a system of geometric conditions and studies when exact concurrency is possible.

sriyantra.cite: Tahta, D. (1992). On the geometry of the sriyantra. The Mathematical Gazette, 76(475), 49–60. doi:10.2307/3620377
sriyantra.why: Examines the yantra's geometric structure and the claims made about it.

infinity.cite: Sathaye, A. (2015). Bhāskarācārya's treatment of the concept of infinity. Gaṇita Bhāratī, 37(1–2), 55–67.
infinity.why: On khahara (a quantity divided by zero) in the Bījagaṇita, including verse 2.20: adding or subtracting does not change it.

infinity.cite: Gupta, R. C. (1992). The first unenumerable number in Jaina mathematics. Gaṇita Bhāratī, 14(1–4), 11–24.
infinity.why: On the Anuyogadvāra Sūtra's construction of the first 'innumerable' number. (Link: MacTutor overview citing it.)

infinity.cite: O'Connor, J. J., & Robertson, E. F. (2000). Jaina mathematics. MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews.
infinity.why: Overview of the enumerable / innumerable / infinite classes and the five kinds of infinity.

infinity.cite: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.1.1 (pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam …). Commentary: Swami Krishnananda, The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.
infinity.why: The verse of fullness: from the full, the full is taken, and the full remains.

infinity.cite: Cantor, G. (1874). Ueber eine Eigenschaft des Inbegriffes aller reellen algebraischen Zahlen. Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik, 77, 258–262.
infinity.why: The first proof that infinities differ in size.

optimisation.cite: Ramasubramanian, K., & Srinivas, M. D. (2010). Development of calculus in India. In Studies in the History of Indian Mathematics. Hindustan Book Agency. doi:10.1007/978-93-86279-49-1_8
optimisation.why: Discusses Bhāskara II's instantaneous motion and the vanishing of the velocity correction where the equation of centre is extremal (Siddhānta-śiromaṇi).

optimisation.cite: Kingma, D. P., & Ba, J. (2015). Adam: A method for stochastic optimization. International Conference on Learning Representations.
optimisation.why: The optimiser that trains most neural networks.
